name: Fizzing Volcano
hint: Two things from the kitchen cupboard. One is sour.
fact: The acid in vinegar swaps partners with baking soda and releases carbon dioxide. The mixture actually gets colder as it fizzes.

name: Sodium Meets Water
hint: A soft metal kept under oil, and the most ordinary liquid there is.
fact: Sodium tears water apart, releasing hydrogen and so much heat that the metal melts into a racing silver ball. What is left in the water is caustic sodium hydroxide.

name: Lilac Fire
hint: Sodium's bigger, angrier cousin, and water.
fact: Potassium reacts so fast that the hydrogen ignites at once. The lilac colour comes from potassium atoms in the flame.

name: The Patient Alkali
hint: The lightest metal, in water.
fact: Lithium releases more energy per atom than sodium, but it reacts slowly and does not melt, so it just fizzes steadily.

name: Milky Water
hint: A hard grey metal from the same family as magnesium, in water.
fact: Calcium bubbles hydrogen and leaves calcium hydroxide, which barely dissolves and turns the water cloudy.

name: Gentle Sodium
hint: Sodium again, but in something you could set on fire.
fact: Alcohols react with sodium the same way water does, only calmly. Chemists use this to destroy leftover sodium safely.

name: Elephant Toothpaste
hint: A pharmacy bottle, something from the bakery, and a squirt of dish soap.
fact: Yeast contains catalase, an enzyme that splits peroxide into water and oxygen. Dish soap traps the oxygen in bubbles, so it climbs out of the container like toothpaste.

name: Neutralisation
hint: An acid and a base cancel out.
fact: Acid plus base gives salt plus water, and always gives off heat.

name: Metal Eats Acid
hint: A reactive metal ribbon in something sour.
fact: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series push hydrogen out of acids. Copper and gold cannot.

name: Rising Agent
hint: Heat the white powder that makes cakes rise.
fact: Above about 100 C baking soda breaks down and releases carbon dioxide and steam, leaving washing soda behind.

name: Caramel
hint: Heat something sweet, gently.
fact: Caramelisation is sugar breaking down by heat alone. No other ingredient is involved.

name: Burnt Offering
hint: Keep heating the caramel.
fact: Strip the water out of sugar and what remains is nearly pure carbon.

name: White Fire
hint: A silvery ribbon held in a flame until it catches.
fact: Magnesium burns at about 3000 C with a light so bright it was used for early flash photography. It keeps burning in carbon dioxide and steam, so water makes it worse.

name: Flash Powder
hint: A kitchen metal will burn, but only as a fine powder and only when very hot.
fact: A lump of aluminium is protected by its oxide skin. Fine powder has so much surface that it burns in a flash.

name: Iron Sulfide
hint: Grey filings and yellow powder, mixed and heated hard.
fact: Once it starts, the reaction makes its own heat and a red glow creeps through the mixture.

name: Glowing Charcoal
hint: The black element, and a flame.
fact: Charcoal burns without much flame because it is nearly pure carbon with nothing to vaporise.

name: Blue Flame
hint: Burn the yellow powder.
fact: Sulfur burns with a ghostly blue flame and makes sulfur dioxide, the choking gas from struck matches.

name: White Smoke
hint: A dark red powder, heated past 260 C.
fact: Burning phosphorus makes a dense white smoke of phosphorus pentoxide. Military smoke screens work the same way.

name: Spirit Flame
hint: A clear liquid that is not water, and a spark.
fact: Ethanol burns cleanly to carbon dioxide and water. The pale blue flame is almost invisible in bright light.

name: Black Copper
hint: Heat the orange metal in air.
fact: The black coat on heated copper is copper oxide. Hot hydrogen can turn it back into shiny metal.

name: Rust
hint: Grey filings, water, air and patience. Salt helps.
fact: Rusting is slow burning. The same reaction that takes years on a bridge powers disposable hand warmers.

name: Squeaky Pop
hint: Collect the gas from a fizzing metal and bring a flame.
fact: Hydrogen and oxygen make water with a bang. A small sample gives the squeaky pop every chemistry student knows.

name: Oil Floats on Water
hint: Two liquids that refuse to mix.
fact: Oil is about 8% less dense than water, and water molecules prefer each other's company.

name: Dissolving
hint: Stir a white crystal into water.
fact: The solid has not vanished. Its particles are spread out among the water molecules, and the mass is all still there.

name: Saturated Solution
hint: Keep adding until no more will dissolve.
fact: Every solid has a limit. For salt it is about 36 g per 100 mL of water.

name: Oobleck
hint: About two parts cornstarch to one part water.
fact: Oobleck is a shear-thickening fluid. Move slowly and it flows; hit it and it locks solid.

name: Red Means Acid
hint: Add indicator to something sour.
fact: Acids have a pH below 7. Vinegar is about pH 2.4.

name: Purple Means Alkali
hint: Add indicator to what sodium leaves behind in water.
fact: Strong bases push the pH toward 14. Sodium hydroxide solution is caustic enough to dissolve hair.

name: Green Means Neutral
hint: Add indicator to plain water.
fact: Pure water sits at pH 7, exactly between acid and base.

name: Boiling Point
hint: Heat water and watch the thermometer stop climbing.
fact: Boiling water stays at 100 C however hard you heat it. The extra energy goes into making steam.

name: Crystals from Brine
hint: Boil salt water until it is dry.
fact: Evaporating the water leaves the dissolved salt behind. This is how sea salt is made.

name: Melting Point
hint: Heat a solid until it gives up.
fact: Every pure substance melts at its own fixed temperature, which is one way chemists identify it.

name: Red Hot
hint: Heat a piece of metal until it glows.
fact: Everything glows the same colour at the same temperature: dull red near 550 C, orange near 900 C, white above 1300 C.

name: Sink or Float
hint: Drop a solid into a liquid.
fact: An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid. Lithium floats on oil; gold sinks in everything.

name: Iron Floats
hint: There is one liquid on the shelf that iron floats on.
fact: Mercury is 13.5 times denser than water. Iron, copper and even lead float on it.

name: Nothing Happens
hint: Try the yellow metal in anything at all.
fact: Gold is so unreactive that it is found in nature as pure metal.

name: Many Smaller Glasses
hint: Glassware and gravity.
fact: Glass breaks when an impact puts more energy into it than its surface cracks can absorb.

name: First Explosion
hint: Too much of a good thing, plus a spark.
fact: An explosion is just a fast reaction that makes hot gas faster than it can get out of the way.

name: Unstable Mystery Mixture
hint: Mix five or more things that have no business together.
fact: Real chemists call this 'the waste beaker'.
